claim: Western blot analysis revealed activation of NF-κB in the corneal tissues of standard housed mice, as indicated by the presence of p-RelA and p-IKKα.
source: Western blot analysis revealed activation of NF-κB in the corneal tissues of standard housed mice, as indicated by the presence of p-RelA and p-IKKα (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating p-RelA and p-IKKα protein levels.

claim: Immunohistochemical staining confirmed nuclear accumulation of RelA in the central region but not much in peripheral or limbal epithelial cells.
source: Immunohistochemical staining confirmed nuclear accumulation of RelA in the central region but not much in peripheral or limbal epithelial cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Activation of NF-κB signaling was also observed in corneal stromal cells, although to a reduced extent.
source: Activation of NF-κB signaling was also observed in corneal stromal cells, although to a reduced extent (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NF-κB activation was increased in both epithelial and stromal cells after alkaline burn.
source: NF-κB activation was increased in both epithelial and stromal cells after alkaline burn (Figure 1A, B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot and immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 1A, B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The basal activity of NF-κB is low but activated during wound healing.
source: This finding is consistent with the notion that the basal activity of NF-κB is low but activated during wound healing (Zhang et al., 2017) and suggests that NF-κB is involved in corneal regeneration.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: NF-κB is involved in corneal regeneration.
source: This finding is consistent with the notion that the basal activity of NF-κB is low but activated during wound healing (Zhang et al., 2017) and suggests that NF-κB is involved in corneal regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NF-κB is activated during wound healing.

claim: The corneas of young Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice appeared normal up to 6 weeks of age.
source: The corneas of young Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice appeared normal up to 6 weeks of age (Figure 1C , D), suggesting that the canonical NF-κB pathway is dispensable for corneal epithelial development and early postnatal growth.
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 1C, D.

claim: The canonical NF-κB pathway is dispensable for corneal epithelial development and early postnatal growth.
source: The corneas of young Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice appeared normal up to 6 weeks of age (Figure 1C , D), suggesting that the canonical NF-κB pathway is dispensable for corneal epithelial development and early postnatal growth.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that young Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice have normal corneas up to 6 weeks of age.

claim: Expression of K14 was not affected in central or peripheral cornea or the limbus in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: In the mutant mice, expression of K14, a CESC marker, was not affected in central or peripheral cornea or the limbus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that the genetic manipulation of the Krt14 or Rela locus or Rela ablation does not affect K14 expression.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Genetic manipulation of the Krt14 or Rela locus or Rela ablation does not affect K14 expression.
source: In the mutant mice, expression of K14, a CESC marker, was not affected in central or peripheral cornea or the limbus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that the genetic manipulation of the Krt14 or Rela locus or Rela ablation does not affect K14 expression.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that K14 expression is not affected in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.

claim: When 4-week-old Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice were subjected to alkaline burn on the ocular surface, severe defects in corneal wound healing were observed.
source: When 4-week-old Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice were subjected to alkaline burn on the ocular surface, severe defects in corneal wound healing were observed (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The regenerated corneal epithelium in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice lacked a basal layer and epithelial basement membrane.
source: Unlike the controls, the regenerated corneal epithelium lacked a basal layer and epithelial basement membrane (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Immunostaining revealed the absence of differentiation marker K12, decreased numbers of PCNA+ proliferating cells, and disrupted Laminin+ basement membrane at the injury sites in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: Immunostaining revealed the absence of differentiation marker K12, decreased numbers of PCNA+ proliferating cells, and disrupted Laminin+ basement membrane at the injury sites, although these anomalies were not observed in the peripheral or limbal epithelia (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Rela ablation impairs central corneal epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation during regeneration.
source: Overall, these results indicate that Rela ablation impairs central corneal epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation during regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice show defects in corneal wound healing.

claim: Prrx1 marked most corneal stromal cells.
source: Our genetic tracing with Prrx1-Cre; ROSA26fs-tdTomato mice revealed that Prrx1 marked most corneal stromal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Prrx1-Cre; Relaf/f mice had a normal corneal structure.
source: Prrx1-Cre; Relaf/f mice had a normal corneal structure, and the healing process after alkaline burn injury was normal compared to that of controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, C.

claim: The healing process after alkaline burn injury was normal in Prrx1-Cre; Relaf/f mice compared to that of controls.
source: Prrx1-Cre; Relaf/f mice had a normal corneal structure, and the healing process after alkaline burn injury was normal compared to that of controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, C.

claim: Deletion of Ikkb in keratocytes (via Keratocan-Cre) impaired corneal repair but not maintenance.
source: A previous study showed that the deletion of Ikkb, which encodes a kinase required for activation of both canonical and noncanonical NF-κB pathways, in keratocytes (via Keratocan-Cre) impaired corneal repair but not maintenance (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: The non-canonical rather than the canonical NF-κB pathway in stromal cells plays a role in corneal regeneration.
source: These results suggest that the non-canonical rather than the canonical NF-κB pathway in stromal cells plays a role in corneal regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Prrx1-Cre; Relaf/f mice have normal corneal structure and healing, while Ikkb deletion impairs corneal repair.

claim: Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice showed visible plaques at the central cornea by 6 months of age.
source: Further analysis of Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice revealed age-dependent changes in corneal structures, including visible plaques at the central cornea by 6 months of age (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by macroscopic images shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The mutant mice had largely normal corneas up to 1.5 months of age.
source: Histological analysis showed that the mutant mice had largely normal corneas up to 1.5 months of age. However, at 2 months of age, the mutant mice showed basal cell atrophy at the central cornea, and the degenerative changes expanded to suprabasal cells at the age of 2.5 months (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At 2 months of age, the mutant mice showed basal cell atrophy at the central cornea.
source: Histological analysis showed that the mutant mice had largely normal corneas up to 1.5 months of age. However, at 2 months of age, the mutant mice showed basal cell atrophy at the central cornea, and the degenerative changes expanded to suprabasal cells at the age of 2.5 months (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The degenerative changes expanded to suprabasal cells at the age of 2.5 months.
source: Histological analysis showed that the mutant mice had largely normal corneas up to 1.5 months of age. However, at 2 months of age, the mutant mice showed basal cell atrophy at the central cornea, and the degenerative changes expanded to suprabasal cells at the age of 2.5 months (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: By 3 months of age, the central corneal epithelium had disappeared in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: By 3 months of age, the central corneal epithelium had disappeared.
evidence: Inferred from the histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In 2-month-old mutant mice, the central cornea had fewer PCNA+ or p63+ cells.
source: In 2-month-old mutant mice, the central cornea had fewer PCNA+ or p63+ cells and showed decreased expression of K12 at the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and qPCR data shown in Figure 2C–E.

claim: In 2-month-old mutant mice, the central cornea showed decreased expression of K12 at the mRNA and protein levels.
source: In 2-month-old mutant mice, the central cornea had fewer PCNA+ or p63+ cells and showed decreased expression of K12 at the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and qPCR data shown in Figure 2C–E.

claim: The number of apoptotic cells remained similar between the mutant and control mice.
source: However, the number of apoptotic cells, which were mainly detected at the central region, remained similar between the mutant and control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The integrity of the epithelial layer was disrupted as the corneal epithelial layer could be scraped off more easily in mutant mice than in control mice.
source: The integrity of the epithelial layer was disrupted as the corneal epithelial layer could be scraped off more easily in mutant mice than in control mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by corneal fragility assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Drastic LC-biotin diffusion from outside the epithelial layer into the stroma was observed in 2- but not 1-month-old mutant mice.
source: In addition, we observed drastic LC-biotin diffusion from outside the epithelial layer into the stroma in 2- but not 1-month-old mutant mice (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by LC-biotin staining assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The peripheral and limbal regions appeared unaltered in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: Interestingly, the peripheral and limbal regions appeared unaltered in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and the numbers of PCNA+ proliferating cells and p63+ CESCs were similar to those of control mice (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: RelA is required for corneal epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation mainly at the central cornea under homeostatic and repair conditions.
source: Overall, these findings indicate that RelA is required for corneal epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation mainly at the central cornea under homeostatic and repair conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Rela ablation causes defects mainly at the central cornea.

claim: Greater activation of NF-κB in the central cornea than the peripheral cornea and limbus may be caused by constant exposure of the central cornea to external environment.
source: This is consistent with greater activation of NF-κB in the central cornea than the peripheral cornea and limbus (Figure 1B), which may be caused by constant exposure of the central cornea to external environment.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the cause of differential NF-κB activation.

claim: Beginning at 3 months of age, keratocyte hyperproliferation, leukocyte infiltration, and generation of blood and lymphatic channels were found in the mutant mice, which progressed with advancing age.
source: Beginning at 3 months of age, we found keratocyte hyperproliferation, leukocyte infiltration, and generation of blood and lymphatic channels, which progressed with advancing age.
evidence: Inferred from histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Immunofluorescent staining revealed cells that stained positive for CD31, Lyve1, or CD45 in the stroma.
source: Immunofluorescent staining further supported the histological results, with the observation of cells that stained positive for CD31, Lyve1, or CD45 in the stroma (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent staining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The stromal cells expressed high levels of vimentin but not αSMA.
source: The stromal cells expressed high levels of vimentin (a fibroblast marker) but not αSMA (a myofibroblast and smooth muscle marker) (Medeiros et al., 2018).
evidence: Inferred from immunofluorescent staining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The stromal cells showed increased expression of fibroblast-specific protein 1 (FSP1) and increased Picrosirius red staining signals.
source: It also showed increased expression of fibroblast-specific protein 1 (FSP1) and increased Picrosirius red staining signals (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent staining and Picrosirius red staining data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stroma expansion was not typical fibrosis in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: These results suggest that stroma expansion was not typical fibrosis in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that stromal cells express vimentin but not αSMA.

claim: Stromal remodeling has been observed in mouse models fed a vitamin A-deficient diet or with epithelial-specific Notch1 ablation.
source: Stromal remodeling has been observed in mouse models fed a vitamin A-deficient diet or with epithelial-specific Notch1 ablation (Toshino et al., 2005; Nowell et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Toshino et al., 2005 and Nowell et al., 2016.

claim: In Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice, stroma remodeling was likely secondary to deterioration of the epithelial layer as it only occurred after 3 months of age when the epithelial layer had been disrupted.
source: In Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice, stroma remodeling was likely secondary to deterioration of the epithelial layer as it only occurred after 3 months of age when the epithelial layer had been disrupted (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from the temporal sequence of events shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A new layer of epithelium formed at 5 months of age in the mutant mice.
source: Intriguingly, a new layer of epithelium formed at 5 months of age in the mutant mice.
evidence: Inferred from histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: By 6 months, the central cornea was covered by a thick layer of keratin and epithelium with invagination into the underlying stroma.
source: By 6 months, the central cornea was covered by a thick layer of keratin and epithelium with invagination into the underlying stroma (Figure 2B), which are features characteristic of hyperproliferative skin.
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: More basal cells and cells immediately above the basal cells, but not limbal cells, were positive for PCNA in 6-month-old mutant mice.
source: This finding is consistent with our observation that more basal cells and cells immediately above the basal cells, but not limbal cells, were positive for PCNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The most highly enriched genes in the mutant samples were epidermal-related genes, in addition to protein synthesis and cell cycle genes.
source: We found that the most highly enriched genes in the mutant samples were epidermal-related genes, in addition to protein synthesis and cell cycle genes (Figure 3D, E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D, E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Immunostaining confirmed the switch from the expression of corneal epithelium-specific K12 to epidermal-specific K1 and loss of Pax6 expression.
source: Immunostaining confirmed the switch from the expression of corneal epithelium-specific K12 to epidermal-specific K1 and loss of Pax6 expression (Figure 3F), confirming the occurrence of metaplasia in corneal epithelial cells.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Metaplasia occurred in corneal epithelial cells in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: Immunostaining confirmed the switch from the expression of corneal epithelium-specific K12 to epidermal-specific K1 and loss of Pax6 expression (Figure 3F), confirming the occurrence of metaplasia in corneal epithelial cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that K12 expression is lost and K1 expression is gained.

claim: Tracing at 6 months of age revealed that the excessively proliferative dermal-like cells were all Tomato+ in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f; ROSA26 fs-tdTomato mice.
source: Tracing at 6 months of age revealed that the excessively proliferative dermal-like cells were all Tomato+ (Figure 3G), indicating that these cells were derived from either the remaining K14+ cells at the central cornea or K14+ cells at the peripheral cornea.
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The excessively proliferative dermal-like cells were derived from either the remaining K14+ cells at the central cornea or K14+ cells at the peripheral cornea.
source: Tracing at 6 months of age revealed that the excessively proliferative dermal-like cells were all Tomato+ (Figure 3G), indicating that these cells were derived from either the remaining K14+ cells at the central cornea or K14+ cells at the peripheral cornea.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all dermal-like cells are Tomato+.

claim: Corneal cell metaplasia has been observed in mouse models of chronic inflammation, Pax6-deficient mice, or in mice fed a vitamin A-deficient diet.
source: Corneal cell metaplasia has been observed in mouse models of chronic inflammation, Pax6-deficient mice, or in mice fed a vitamin A-deficient diet and is believed to occur in stem cells or progenitor cells (Ouyang et al., 2014; Vauclair et al., 2007; Nowell et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ouyang et al., 2014; Vauclair et al., 2007; Nowell et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2009.

claim: Corneal cell metaplasia is believed to occur in stem cells or progenitor cells.
source: Corneal cell metaplasia has been observed in mouse models of chronic inflammation, Pax6-deficient mice, or in mice fed a vitamin A-deficient diet and is believed to occur in stem cells or progenitor cells (Ouyang et al., 2014; Vauclair et al., 2007; Nowell et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ouyang et al., 2014; Vauclair et al., 2007; Nowell et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2009.

claim: Epidermal-like cells originate from corneal epithelial progenitors, which undergo metaplastic changes in the central region in the presence of remodeling stroma in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that epidermal-like cells originate from corneal epithelial progenitors, which undergo metaplastic changes in the central region in the presence of remodeling stroma in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
evidence: Inferred from lineage tracing and histological data.

claim: Rela ablation did not affect conjunctiva or meibomian glands, as well as the overall structure of the skin, oral mucosa, trachea, or intestine epithelia.
source: Although genetic tracing showed the presence of K14-labeled epithelial cells in the conjunctiva, meibomian glands, and epithelial cells of many other organs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B), Rela ablation did not affect conjunctiva or meibomian glands, as well as the overall structure of the skin, oral mucosa, trachea, or intestine epithelia (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–C.

claim: The effects of RelA are restricted to the central cornea, which may be caused by mitogenic signals secreted by the remodeling stroma, in cooperation with environmental cues.
source: These results suggest that the effects of RelA are restricted to the central cornea, which may be caused by mitogenic signals secreted by the remodeling stroma, in cooperation with environmental cues.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the cause of restricted effects of RelA.

claim: Rela-/- cells showed drastic defects in proliferation, as indicated by a reduction in the number of PCNA+ cells.
source: We found that Rela-/- cells showed drastic defects in proliferation, as indicated by a reduction in the number of PCNA+ cells, and differentiation, as indicated by decreased expression of K12 at the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cell culture data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Rela-/- cells showed defects in differentiation, as indicated by decreased expression of K12 at the mRNA and protein levels.
source: We found that Rela-/- cells showed drastic defects in proliferation, as indicated by a reduction in the number of PCNA+ cells, and differentiation, as indicated by decreased expression of K12 at the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cell culture data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The epidermal markers K1 and K10 were not detectable in Rela-/- or control cultures.
source: However, the epidermal markers K1 and K10 were not detectable in Rela-/- or control cultures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RelA plays positive roles in corneal epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation.
source: These results confirm the positive roles of RelA in corneal epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation and suggest that the subsequent epidermal conversion and plaque formation may not be cell autonomous.
evidence: Inferred from in vitro cell culture data.

claim: The subsequent epidermal conversion and plaque formation may not be cell autonomous.
source: These results confirm the positive roles of RelA in corneal epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation and suggest that the subsequent epidermal conversion and plaque formation may not be cell autonomous.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that K1 and K10 are not detectable in Rela-/- cultures.

claim: Niche molecules provided by the stroma may play an important role in epidermal conversion and plaque formation.
source: Rather, niche molecules provided by the stroma may play an important role in these events.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the role of stromal niche molecules.

claim: Rela ablation led to a severe reduction in the expression of the RA synthesis enzyme Aldh1a1.
source: Gene ontology (GO) and kyoto encyclopedia of genes and genomes (KEGG) analyses revealed that Rela ablation led to a severe reduction in the expression of the RA synthesis enzyme Aldh1a1, as well as pathways that control cell proliferation, wound healing, and inflammation (Figure 4B, C), consistent with our in vivo results.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: Rela ablation led to a reduction in pathways that control cell proliferation, wound healing, and inflammation.
source: Gene ontology (GO) and kyoto encyclopedia of genes and genomes (KEGG) analyses revealed that Rela ablation led to a severe reduction in the expression of the RA synthesis enzyme Aldh1a1, as well as pathways that control cell proliferation, wound healing, and inflammation (Figure 4B, C), consistent with our in vivo results.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: RA is synthesized from vitamin A via two steps, and the first step is catalyzed by ADH/RDH, while the second step is catalyzed by Aldh1a1-3.
source: RA is synthesized from vitamin A via two steps, and the first step is catalyzed by ADH/RDH, while the second step is catalyzed by Aldh1a1-3 (Ghyselinck and Duester, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ghyselinck and Duester, 2019.

claim: RA binds to RA receptors (RARs) and RA X receptors (RXRs) to control gene expression.
source: RA binds to RA receptors (RARs) and RA X receptors (RXRs) to control gene expression.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about RA signaling.

claim: RA is known to play important roles in corneal development and epithelial cell differentiation.
source: RA is known to play important roles in corneal development and epithelial cell differentiation, and vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, corneal ulcers, and keratomalacia, mainly in children (Kastner et al., 1994; Lassen et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2012; Macsai et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kastner et al., 1994; Lassen et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2012; Macsai et al., 1998.

claim: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, corneal ulcers, and keratomalacia, mainly in children.
source: RA is known to play important roles in corneal development and epithelial cell differentiation, and vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, corneal ulcers, and keratomalacia, mainly in children (Kastner et al., 1994; Lassen et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2012; Macsai et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kastner et al., 1994; Lassen et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2012; Macsai et al., 1998.

claim: Whole-body deletion of Aldh1a genes causes xerophthalmia, as well as thinning of the stromal layer in young mice, which is followed by reduced proliferation and increased apoptosis of epithelial cells.
source: Whole-body deletion of Aldh1a genes causes xerophthalmia, as well as thinning of the stromal layer in young mice, which is followed by reduced proliferation and increased apoptosis of epithelial cells (Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kumar et al., 2017.

claim: The mRNA levels Aldh1a1 were decreased in Rela-deficient corneal samples.
source: We confirmed that the mRNA levels Aldh1a1 were decreased in Rela-deficient corneal samples (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Western blot and immunostaining confirmed decreased Aldh1a1 expression at the protein level in Rela-deficient samples.
source: Western blot and immunostaining confirmed decreased Aldh1a1 expression at the protein level in Rela-deficient samples (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: Supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 4E, F.

claim: RA synthesis is defective in the corneas of Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: These results suggest that RA synthesis is defective in the corneas of Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Aldh1a1 expression is decreased in Rela-deficient samples.

claim: Immunostaining revealed reduced expression of Aldh1a1 in the limbus and conjunctiva.
source: Immunostaining revealed reduced expression of Aldh1a1 in the limbus and conjunctiva while the meibomian glands do not express Aldh1a1 (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The meibomian glands do not express Aldh1a1.
source: Immunostaining revealed reduced expression of Aldh1a1 in the limbus and conjunctiva while the meibomian glands do not express Aldh1a1 (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The function of RA is restricted to the central cornea.
source: The observation that the limbus and conjunctiva did not show obvious defects in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice indicates that the function of RA is also restricted to the central cornea.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that limbus and conjunctiva do not show defects despite reduced Aldh1a1 expression.

claim: The promoter of Aldh1a1 contained a putative NF-κB binding site (G/CGGA/GATTTCC) between −1164 and −1155.
source: Furthermore, we found that the promoter of Aldh1a1 contained a putative NF-κB binding site (G/CGGA/GATTTCC) between −1164 and −1155 (Figure 4G, H).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4G, H.

claim: ChIP results verified the presence of the NF-κB binding site in the Aldh1a1 promoter.
source: The ChIP results verified the presence of the NF-κB binding site in the Aldh1a1 promoter (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: RelA directly regulates Aldh1a1 expression in corneal epithelial cells.
source: Overall, these findings indicate that RelA directly regulates Aldh1a1 expression in corneal epithelial cells.
evidence: Inferred from ChIP assay data showing RelA binding to Aldh1a1 promoter.

claim: The defects in cell proliferation and differentiation in cultured Rela-/- corneal epithelial cells were rescued by adding RA to the medium.
source: In cultured Rela-/- corneal epithelial cells, we found that the defects in cell proliferation and differentiation were rescued by adding RA to the medium (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cell culture data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Addition of an RA receptor inhibitor impaired cell proliferation and differentiation in cultures of normal corneal epithelial cells.
source: Moreover, in cultures of normal corneal epithelial cells, addition of an RA receptor inhibitor impaired cell proliferation and differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cell culture data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: RA mediates the effect of Rela deletion on corneal epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation.
source: These results indicate that RA mediates the effect of Rela deletion on corneal epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from in vitro cell culture data showing RA rescue of Rela-/- cell defects.

claim: No corneal plaques were seen in RA-treated Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: Macroscopically, no corneal plaques were seen in RA-treated mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by macroscopic images shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 6-month-old RA-treated mutant mice showed normal corneal epithelial and stromal structures.
source: Histological and immunological analyses revealed that 6-month-old RA-treated mutant mice showed normal corneal epithelial and stromal structures (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Supported by histological and immunological data shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: 1.5 months of RA treatment, starting at 1.5 months of age, prevented thinning and dissolution of the epithelial layer at the central cornea.
source: In addition, 1.5 months of RA treatment, starting at 1.5 months of age, prevented thinning and dissolution of the epithelial layer at the central cornea (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A reduction in RA synthesis mediates the defects in the central cornea caused by Rela ablation.
source: These results suggest that a reduction in RA synthesis mediates the defects in the central cornea caused by Rela ablation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RA treatment rescues corneal defects in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.

claim: RA-treated mutant mice were able to regenerate the epithelial layer as effectively as normal mice after alkaline-induced injury.
source: Moreover, when we administered RA to 4-week-old Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f and control mice with alkaline-induced injury, RA-treated mutant mice were able to regenerate the epithelial layer as effectively as normal mice (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 5E, F.

claim: Canonical NF-κB signaling regulates corneal epithelial homeostasis and regeneration by promoting RA synthesis.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that canonical NF-κB signaling regulates corneal epithelial homeostasis and regeneration by promoting RA synthesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RA treatment rescues corneal defects in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.

claim: Treatment of Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f with RA at 3 months of age, after epithelial layer disruption, failed to prevent central corneal epithelial cell metaplasia, stromal remodeling, and plaque development.
source: However, treatment of Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f with RA at 3 months of age, after epithelial layer disruption, failed to prevent central corneal epithelial cell metaplasia, stromal remodeling, and plaque development (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), indicating that RA could not reverse corneal epithelial metaplasia.
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RA could not reverse corneal epithelial metaplasia.
source: However, treatment of Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f with RA at 3 months of age, after epithelial layer disruption, failed to prevent central corneal epithelial cell metaplasia, stromal remodeling, and plaque development (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), indicating that RA could not reverse corneal epithelial metaplasia.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RA treatment at 3 months of age does not prevent metaplasia.

claim: The primary epithelial defects (deterioration) caused by Rela deletion are attributable to a reduction in RA synthesis.
source: Overall, these findings suggest that the primary epithelial defects (deterioration) caused by Rela deletion are attributable to a reduction in RA synthesis, whereas epithelial metaplasia and plaque formation are not directly caused by RA deficiency.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RA treatment rescues early epithelial defects but not metaplasia.

claim: Epithelial metaplasia and plaque formation are not directly caused by RA deficiency.
source: Overall, these findings suggest that the primary epithelial defects (deterioration) caused by Rela deletion are attributable to a reduction in RA synthesis, whereas epithelial metaplasia and plaque formation are not directly caused by RA deficiency.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RA treatment at 3 months of age does not prevent metaplasia.

claim: The stroma showed an increase in expression of Vegfa but not Vegfb, Vegfc, or Vegfd in 3-month-old Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: Consistent with new blood vessel formation, the stroma showed an increase in expression of Vegfa but not Vegfb, Vegfc, or Vegfd in 3-month-old Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Axitinib not only prevented corneal angiogenesis but also suppressed epithelial cell overproliferation and metaplasia.
source: Axitinib not only prevented corneal angiogenesis but also suppressed epithelial cell overproliferation and metaplasia (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), confirming the importance of VEGFA-VEGFR in these events.
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: VEGFA-VEGFR is important in corneal angiogenesis, epithelial cell overproliferation, and metaplasia.
source: Axitinib not only prevented corneal angiogenesis but also suppressed epithelial cell overproliferation and metaplasia (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), confirming the importance of VEGFA-VEGFR in these events.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that axitinib prevents angiogenesis, overproliferation, and metaplasia.

claim: The central corneal epithelial layer remained disrupted in axitinib-treated mice, accompanied by decreased cell proliferation.
source: However, the central corneal epithelial layer remained disrupted, accompanied by decreased cell proliferation, with the epithelial layer being similar to that of 3-month-old Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice without treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and Figure 2B.

claim: Axitinib did not affect development of early corneal epithelial defects caused by RelA ablation.
source: The results suggested that axitinib did not affect development of early corneal epithelial defects caused by RelA ablation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the epithelial layer remains disrupted in axitinib-treated mice.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed enhanced activation of the mitogenic Erk and Stat3 pathways but not Akt1 or β-catenin in corneal samples of 6-month-old Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: Consistent with hyperproliferation of metaplastic cells, western blot analysis revealed enhanced activation of the mitogenic Erk and Stat3 pathways but not Akt1 or β-catenin in corneal samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Enhanced phosphorylation of EGFRs was found in the skin-like epithelial tissue of 6-month-old Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: While VEGFA secreted by the stroma may contribute to activation of some of these signaling molecules, we found enhanced phosphorylation of EGFRs in the skin-like epithelial tissue (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), which has an established role in corneal epithelial cell proliferation (McClintock and Ceresa, 2010).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: EGFR has an established role in corneal epithelial cell proliferation.
source: While VEGFA secreted by the stroma may contribute to activation of some of these signaling molecules, we found enhanced phosphorylation of EGFRs in the skin-like epithelial tissue (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), which has an established role in corneal epithelial cell proliferation (McClintock and Ceresa, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to McClintock and Ceresa, 2010.

claim: Immunostaining confirmed activation of EGFR, as well as Erk and Stat3 in metaplastic cells.
source: Immunostaining confirmed activation of EGFR, as well as Erk and Stat3 in metaplastic cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: EGFs might be synthesized by remodeling stromal cells or brought in by newly formed blood vessels via blood circulation.
source: EGFs might be synthesized by remodeling stromal cells or brought in by newly formed blood vessels via blood circulation as it is well known that plasma contains high levels of EGF molecules (Sánchez-Vizcaíno et al., 2010).
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the source of EGFs, supported by citation to Sánchez-Vizcaíno et al., 2010.

claim: Plasma contains high levels of EGF molecules.
source: EGFs might be synthesized by remodeling stromal cells or brought in by newly formed blood vessels via blood circulation as it is well known that plasma contains high levels of EGF molecules (Sánchez-Vizcaíno et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sánchez-Vizcaíno et al., 2010.

claim: Immune cell infiltration was largely blocked by levofloxacin treatment in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: While immune cell infiltration was largely blocked, stroma remodeling, angiogenesis, epidermal fate conversion, and plaque formation were not obviously affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4A, B.

claim: Stroma remodeling, angiogenesis, epidermal fate conversion, and plaque formation were not obviously affected by levofloxacin treatment in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: While immune cell infiltration was largely blocked, stroma remodeling, angiogenesis, epidermal fate conversion, and plaque formation were not obviously affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4A, B.

claim: Levofloxacin treatment did not affect NF-κB activation during regeneration in normal mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that levofloxacin treatment did not affect NF-κB activation during regeneration in normal mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Bacterial infection plays a minimal role in corneal defects of Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: These results indicate that bacterial infection plays a minimal role in corneal defects of Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that levofloxacin treatment does not prevent corneal defects.

claim: Approximately 12% of 24-month-old normal mice showed thinning of the corneal epithelial layer.
source: Approximately 12% of 24-month-old normal mice showed thinning of the corneal epithelial layer (hereafter designated moderate anomaly), 28% of mice showed epithelial overgrowth and plaque formation at the central cornea (hereafter designated severe anomaly), although 20-month-old mice showed no changes (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: 28% of 24-month-old normal mice showed epithelial overgrowth and plaque formation at the central cornea.
source: Approximately 12% of 24-month-old normal mice showed thinning of the corneal epithelial layer (hereafter designated moderate anomaly), 28% of mice showed epithelial overgrowth and plaque formation at the central cornea (hereafter designated severe anomaly), although 20-month-old mice showed no changes (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: 20-month-old mice showed no changes in corneal structure.
source: Approximately 12% of 24-month-old normal mice showed thinning of the corneal epithelial layer (hereafter designated moderate anomaly), 28% of mice showed epithelial overgrowth and plaque formation at the central cornea (hereafter designated severe anomaly), although 20-month-old mice showed no changes (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: Only a portion of aged mice showed corneal anomalies, suggesting the involvement of environmental factors in corneal aging.
source: The observation that only a portion of aged mice showed corneal anomalies suggests the involvement of environmental factors in corneal aging.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that not all aged mice show corneal anomalies.

claim: Thinning of the epithelial layer precedes plaque formation in aged mice.
source: It is possible that thinning of the epithelial layer precedes plaque formation in aged mice.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the temporal sequence of events in aged mice.

claim: The thin corneal epithelium of 24-month-old mice showed a decrease in the numbers of proliferating cells and p63+ CESCs.
source: The thin corneal epithelium of 24-month-old mice showed a decrease in the numbers of proliferating cells and p63+ CESCs and decreased expression of K12 and Pax6 but no change in apoptotic cells (Figure 6C, D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C, D.

claim: The thin corneal epithelium of 24-month-old mice showed decreased expression of K12 and Pax6.
source: The thin corneal epithelium of 24-month-old mice showed a decrease in the numbers of proliferating cells and p63+ CESCs and decreased expression of K12 and Pax6 but no change in apoptotic cells (Figure 6C, D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C, D.

claim: There was no change in apoptotic cells in the thin corneal epithelium of 24-month-old mice.
source: The thin corneal epithelium of 24-month-old mice showed a decrease in the numbers of proliferating cells and p63+ CESCs and decreased expression of K12 and Pax6 but no change in apoptotic cells (Figure 6C, D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In corneas with plaque formation, the epithelial cells were K1-positive.
source: In corneas with plaque formation, the epithelial cells were K1-positive, and the thickened stroma was positive for FSP1 and vimentin, accompanied by neovascularization, lymphatic vessel formation, and immune cell infiltration (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In corneas with plaque formation, the thickened stroma was positive for FSP1 and vimentin.
source: In corneas with plaque formation, the epithelial cells were K1-positive, and the thickened stroma was positive for FSP1 and vimentin, accompanied by neovascularization, lymphatic vessel formation, and immune cell infiltration (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Corneas with plaque formation showed neovascularization, lymphatic vessel formation, and immune cell infiltration.
source: In corneas with plaque formation, the epithelial cells were K1-positive, and the thickened stroma was positive for FSP1 and vimentin, accompanied by neovascularization, lymphatic vessel formation, and immune cell infiltration (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The peripheral cornea and limbus region appeared normal in both groups of aged mice.
source: However, the peripheral cornea and limbus region appeared normal in both groups of mice (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar changes in corneal thickness and corneal epithelial keratinization have been observed in aged humans, although they do not progress to plaque formation or blindness.
source: Similar changes in corneal thickness and corneal epithelial keratinization have been observed in aged humans, although they do not progress to plaque formation or blindness (Yang et al., 2014; Blackburn et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2014 and Blackburn et al., 2019.

claim: In the thin corneal samples of 24-month-old mice expression of RelA and Aldh1a1 and activation of NF-κB were significantly reduced compared to those of corneal samples from young mice.
source: We found that in the thin corneal samples of 24-month-old mice expression of RelA and Aldh1a1 and activation of NF-κB were significantly reduced compared to those of corneal samples from young mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: qPCR analysis confirmed reduced expression of Rela and Aldh1a1 at the mRNA level in aged mice.
source: qPCR analysis confirmed reduced expression of Rela and Aldh1a1 at the mRNA level (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Immunohistochemical staining of RelA and immunostaining of Aldh1a1 confirmed the reductions in these two proteins in the central cornea of aged mice.
source: Immunohistochemical staining of RelA and immunostaining of Aldh1a1 confirmed the reductions in these two proteins in the central cornea (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining and immunostaining data shown in Figure 7C, D.

claim: None of the RA-treated 20-month-old normal mice developed corneal plaques.
source: None of the RA-treated mice developed corneal plaques, and the percentage of mice with thinned corneas was greatly reduced (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by macroscopic observation data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The percentage of mice with thinned corneas was greatly reduced by RA treatment.
source: None of the RA-treated mice developed corneal plaques, and the percentage of mice with thinned corneas was greatly reduced (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by macroscopic observation data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The alteration in histological structure and expression of epidermal marker genes in the aged cornea was rescued by RA treatment.
source: Moreover, the alteration in histological structure and expression of epidermal marker genes in the aged cornea was also rescued (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by histological and immunostaining data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: A reduction in RA synthesis is involved in age-related corneal degeneration.
source: To examine whether a reduction in RA synthesis is involved in age-related corneal degeneration, we treated 20-month-old normal mice with RA for 4 months and examined their corneas.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RA treatment prevents age-related corneal anomalies.

claim: RA plays a critical role in natural aging of the cornea.
source: These results confirm a critical role of RA in natural aging of the cornea and suggest the RA-containing ointment may be applied to the central cornea to slow down the development of aging-related corneal anomalies.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RA treatment prevents age-related corneal anomalies.

claim: RA-containing ointment may be applied to the central cornea to slow down the development of aging-related corneal anomalies.
source: These results confirm a critical role of RA in natural aging of the cornea and suggest the RA-containing ointment may be applied to the central cornea to slow down the development of aging-related corneal anomalies.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential therapeutic application of RA.

claim: NF-κB is a central player in the inflammatory response and cell proliferation and survival.
source: Many environmental insults to the cornea are potential activators of NF-κB, which is a central player in the inflammatory response and cell proliferation and survival (Taniguchi and Karin, 2018; Eluard et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Taniguchi and Karin, 2018 and Eluard et al., 2020.

claim: Previous studies have reported NF-κB activation in corneal epithelial cells, macrophages, and keratocytes, which is required for cytokine production, corneal regeneration, and fibrosis.
source: Previous studies have reported NF-κB activation in corneal epithelial cells, macrophages, and keratocytes, which is required for cytokine production, corneal regeneration, and fibrosis (Zhou et al., 2021; Nakano et al., 2018; Lennikov et al., 2018; Orita et al., 2013; Oh et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2021; Nakano et al., 2018; Lennikov et al., 2018; Orita et al., 2013; Oh et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2016.

claim: NF-κB activation may promote corneal healing via upregulating the expression of CCCTC-binding factors in epithelial cells.
source: NF-κB activation may promote corneal healing via upregulating the expression of CCCTC-binding factors in epithelial cells (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2013.

claim: This study established NF-κB as a critical regulator of corneal epithelial maintenance and regeneration.
source: In this study, we established NF-κB, which responds to many extracellular stimuli and injury, as a critical regulator of corneal epithelial maintenance and regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the overall findings of the study.

claim: This study uncovered the important mechanisms governing corneal homeostasis and regeneration.
source: This study thus uncovered the important mechanisms governing corneal homeostasis and regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Centrally located CESCs play a role in corneal homeostasis and regeneration.
source: The findings of our study suggest that centrally located CESCs play a role in corneal homeostasis and regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Rela deletion causes defects mainly at the central cornea.

claim: If limbal CESCs were solely responsible for corneal regeneration, exhaustion of limbal CESCs should have occurred in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: If limbal CESCs were solely responsible for corneal regeneration, exhaustion of limbal CESCs should have occurred in Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
evidence: Logical inference about the expected outcome if limbal CESCs were solely responsible for regeneration.

claim: Central CESCs play an important role in corneal homeostasis and regeneration.
source: Overall, these findings indicate that central CESCs play an important role in corneal homeostasis and regeneration (Majo et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2011; Nasser et al., 2018; West, 2015; Sun et al., 2010).
evidence: Inferred from the overall findings of the study, supported by citations to Majo et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2011; Nasser et al., 2018; West, 2015; Sun et al., 2010.

claim: The differential responses to Rela deletion in the central and limbal CESCs are likely due to their distinct niches.
source: The differential responses to Rela deletion in the central and limbal CESCs are likely due to their distinct niches as the central cornea is constantly exposed to the external cues including UV lights, infectious particles, chemicals, and dirt and is under different mechanical strains, compared to limbal cells (Nowell et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the cause of differential responses, supported by citation to Nowell et al., 2016.

claim: Rela ablation does not affect other organs/tissues marked by K14 in mice.
source: Moreover, we show that Rela ablation does not affect other organs/tissues marked by K14 in mice.
evidence: Inferred from histological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: NF-κB promoted corneal epithelial progenitor proliferation and differentiation by controlling RA synthesis.
source: Mechanistically, we showed that NF-κB promoted corneal epithelial progenitor proliferation and differentiation by controlling RA synthesis.
evidence: Inferred from the overall findings of the study.

claim: NF-κB directly regulated the expression of Aldh1a1, a rate-limiting enzyme in the RA synthesis pathway.
source: NF-κB directly regulated the expression of Aldh1a1, a rate-limiting enzyme in the RA synthesis pathway.
evidence: Inferred from ChIP assay data showing RelA binding to Aldh1a1 promoter.

claim: Previous studies have shown that RA plays a role in eye development, likely via the Wnt-β-catenin pathway.
source: Previous studies have shown that RA plays a role in eye development, likely via the Wnt-β-catenin pathway (Smith et al., 2018; Niederreither and Dollé, 2008; Larange and Cheroutre, 2016), which is involved in corneal stromal cells (Kumar and Duester, 2010; Smith et al., 2018; Nowell et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2018; Niederreither and Dollé, 2008; Larange and Cheroutre, 2016; Kumar and Duester, 2010; Nowell et al., 2016.

claim: Vitamin A deficiency in humans causes xerophthalmia, night blindness, corneal ulcers, and other symptoms, especially in children.
source: Vitamin A deficiency in humans causes xerophthalmia, night blindness, corneal ulcers, and other symptoms, especially in children.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about vitamin A deficiency.

claim: This study highlights the importance of RA, a vitamin A metabolite, in maintaining healthy corneas in adults and in preventing corneal aging.
source: Our study highlights the importance of RA, a vitamin A metabolite, in maintaining healthy corneas in adults and in preventing corneal aging.
evidence: Inferred from the overall findings of the study.

claim: RA has been approved to treat skin disorders including psoriasis and acne as well as acute lymphatic leukemia.
source: RA has been approved to treat skin disorders including psoriasis and acne as well as acute lymphatic leukemia (Tang and Gudas, 2011; Ferreira et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tang and Gudas, 2011 and Ferreira et al., 2020.

claim: Ablation of Notch1 in corneal epithelial cells also caused epithelial metaplasia and plaque formation.
source: In addition, ablation of Notch1 in corneal epithelial cells also caused epithelial metaplasia and plaque formation (Vauclair et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vauclair et al., 2007.

claim: The Notch1-deficient mice show a loss of meibomian glands and much reduced expression of retinol transporting protein CRBP1 but no thinning or loss of the epithelial layer compared to Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
source: The Notch1-deficient mice show a loss of meibomian glands and much reduced expression of retinol transporting protein CRBP1 but no thinning or loss of the epithelial layer compared to Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mice.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with published data on Notch1-deficient mice.

claim: Both Notch1-deficient and Krt14-Cre; Relaf/f mouse models underscore the importance of RA pathway in cornea maintenance and regeneration.
source: Despite these differences, both models underscore the importance of RA pathway in cornea maintenance and regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of the two mouse models.

claim: RA appears to play an insignificant role in subsequent wound healing events, including epithelial metaplasia and plaque formation.
source: Notably, RA appears to play an insignificant role in subsequent wound healing events, including epithelial metaplasia and plaque formation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RA treatment at 3 months of age does not prevent metaplasia.

claim: Stroma-secreted VEGF and/or neovascularization play a causal role in epithelial metaplasia and plaque formation.
source: Instead, we showed that stroma-secreted VEGF and/or neovascularization play a causal role in these events.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that axitinib prevents metaplasia and plaque formation.

claim: The findings reinforce the importance of preventing neovascularization in maintaining healthy corneas.
source: Our findings reinforce the importance of preventing neovascularization in maintaining healthy corneas and suggest that in patients already showing corneal epithelial metaplasia VEGFR inhibitors may help to slow the pathological progression.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that axitinib prevents metaplasia and plaque formation.

claim: In patients already showing corneal epithelial metaplasia VEGFR inhibitors may help to slow the pathological progression.
source: Our findings reinforce the importance of preventing neovascularization in maintaining healthy corneas and suggest that in patients already showing corneal epithelial metaplasia VEGFR inhibitors may help to slow the pathological progression.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential therapeutic application of VEGFR inhibitors.

claim: NF-κB signaling plays an anti-aging role in mouse cornea.
source: Our findings indicate that NF-κB signaling plays an anti-aging role in mouse cornea.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that aged mice show reduced NF-κB activation and corneal anomalies.

claim: NF-κB activation can increase the expression of senescence-associated secretory phenotype cytokines, including IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α, which promote inflammation and aging in many tissues.
source: On the other hand, NF-κB activation can increase the expression of senescence-associated secretory phenotype cytokines, including IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α, which promote inflammation and aging in many tissues (Taniguchi and Karin, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taniguchi and Karin, 2018.

claim: The activity of NF-κB must be fine-tuned in corneal epithelial cells.
source: Thus, the activity of NF-κB must be fine-tuned in corneal epithelial cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NF-κB has both beneficial and detrimental effects.

claim: Constant activation of the NF-κB pathway by pro-aging factors may disrupt the regulatory circuits and lead to reduced expression and activation of RelA.
source: Constant activation of the pathway by pro-aging factors, for example, reactive oxygen species and chronic inflammation, may disrupt the regulatory circuits and lead to reduced expression and activation of RelA.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the cause of reduced RelA expression in aged mice.

claim: In human, although corneal epithelia thinning and keratinization have been observed in the elderly, corneal plaque formation and loss of vision rarely occur.
source: In human, although corneal epithelia thinning and keratinization have been observed in the elderly, corneal plaque formation and loss of vision rarely occur (Yang et al., 2014; Blackburn et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2014 and Blackburn et al., 2019.

claim: Aging-related decrease in RA synthesis may be made up for by RA-rich nutrients in humans.
source: One explanation is that aging-related decrease in RA synthesis may be made up for by RA-rich nutrients.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about why humans do not develop severe corneal anomalies with age.

claim: Age-related corneal problems may be diagnosed early and are treated successfully in humans.
source: Alternatively, age-related corneal problems may be diagnosed early and are treated successfully.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about why humans do not develop severe corneal anomalies with age.

claim: This study uncovers the important mechanisms governing corneal epithelium homeostasis, regeneration, and aging.
source: In summary, this study uncovers the important mechanisms governing corneal epithelium homeostasis, regeneration, and aging, and suggests that the canonical NF-κB-RA pathway may be a target to improve corneal health.
evidence: Inferred from the overall findings of the study.

claim: The canonical NF-κB-RA pathway may be a target to improve corneal health.
source: In summary, this study uncovers the important mechanisms governing corneal epithelium homeostasis, regeneration, and aging, and suggests that the canonical NF-κB-RA pathway may be a target to improve corneal health.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential therapeutic target.
